notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Environmental pollution is the introduction of harmful substances or forms of energy into the environment at levels that adversely affect living organisms, ecosystems or human health.
  • Pollution may affect:
  • Air.
  • Water.
  • Soil.
  • Oceans.
  • Living organisms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pollution → Harmful Change in Environmental Quality

2. Pollutant
  • A pollutant is any substance, organism or form of energy that causes undesirable environmental effects.
  • Pollutants may be:
  • Solid.
  • Liquid.
  • Gas.
  • Biological.
  • Radioactive.
  • Thermal.
  • Noise.
3. Natural Sources of Pollution

Natural pollution sources include:

  • Volcanic eruptions.
  • Forest fires.
  • Dust storms.
  • Sea salt.
  • Pollen.
4. Human-Induced Pollution

Major anthropogenic sources include:

  • Industries.
  • Motor vehicles.
  • Fossil-fuel combustion.
  • Agriculture.
  • Mining.
  • Sewage.
  • Solid waste.
5. Primary Pollutant
  • A primary pollutant is emitted directly from a source.

Examples include:

  • Carbon monoxide.
  • Sulphur dioxide.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • Particulate matter.
6. Secondary Pollutant
  • A secondary pollutant forms in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants.

Examples include:

  • Tropospheric ozone.
  • Components of photochemical smog.
  • Some secondary aerosols.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Primary → Emitted Directly

Secondary → Formed by Reactions

7. Point-Source Pollution
  • Point-source pollution originates from an identifiable single source.

Examples:

  • Factory discharge pipe.
  • Sewage outlet.
  • Chimney.
8. Non-Point-Source Pollution
  • Non-point-source pollution comes from widespread diffuse sources.

Examples:

  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Urban runoff.
  • Soil erosion.
9. Major Types of Environmental Pollution

Important types include:

  • Air pollution.
  • Water pollution.
  • Soil pollution.
  • Noise pollution.
  • Thermal pollution.
  • Radioactive pollution.
  • Marine pollution.
  • Light pollution.
10. Air Pollution
  • Air pollution occurs when harmful gases, particles or biological materials contaminate the atmosphere.
  • It can affect:
  • Human health.
  • Crops.
  • Buildings.
  • Climate.
11. Major Air Pollutants

Important air pollutants include:

  • Particulate matter.
  • Sulphur dioxide.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • Carbon monoxide.
  • Ground-level ozone.
  • Volatile organic compounds.
  • Lead.
12. Particulate Matter
  • Particulate matter consists of tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air.
  • It includes:
  • Dust.
  • Smoke.
  • Soot.
  • Aerosols.
13. PM10
  • PM10 refers to particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter up to approximately 10 micrometres.
  • These particles can enter the respiratory system.
14. PM2.5
  • PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter with diameter up to approximately 2.5 micrometres.
  • Fine particles can penetrate deeply into the lungs.
📌 Must-Memorise

PM2.5 → Finer than PM10

15. Sources of Particulate Matter

Sources include:

  • Vehicle exhaust.
  • Coal combustion.
  • Construction dust.
  • Road dust.
  • Biomass burning.
  • Industries.
16. Sulphur Dioxide
  • Sulphur dioxide is produced mainly by burning sulphur-containing fossil fuels.
  • Major sources include:
  • Coal-fired power stations.
  • Industries.
  • Some petroleum fuels.
17. Effects of Sulphur Dioxide

SO₂ can contribute to:

  • Respiratory irritation.
  • Acid rain.
  • Formation of secondary particulate matter.
18. Nitrogen Oxides
  • Nitrogen oxides are produced mainly during high-temperature combustion.
  • Major sources include:
  • Motor vehicles.
  • Thermal power stations.
  • Industrial boilers.
19. Effects of Nitrogen Oxides

NOx contributes to:

  • Photochemical smog.
  • Ground-level ozone.
  • Acid rain.
  • Respiratory problems.
20. Carbon Monoxide
  • Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas.
  • It forms during incomplete combustion.

Sources include:

  • Motor vehicles.
  • Biomass burning.
  • Poorly ventilated combustion.
📌 Must-Memorise

CO → Incomplete Combustion

21. Carbon Monoxide and Health
  • Carbon monoxide binds strongly with haemoglobin.
  • It reduces the blood's ability to transport oxygen.
22. Ground-Level Ozone
  • Tropospheric ozone is a secondary pollutant.
  • It forms through photochemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in sunlight.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ground-Level Ozone → Pollutant

Stratospheric Ozone → Protective

23. Volatile Organic Compounds
  • VOCs are organic compounds that readily evaporate.
  • Sources include:
  • Fuels.
  • Solvents.
  • Paints.
  • Industrial emissions.
24. Lead Pollution

Lead can enter the environment from:

  • Industrial processes.
  • Batteries.
  • Waste recycling.
  • Contaminated dust.

Lead exposure can damage the nervous system.

25. Smog
  • Smog is polluted air containing smoke, gases and aerosols.
  • Two commonly discussed types are:
  • Classical smog.
  • Photochemical smog.
26. Classical Smog
  • Classical smog develops under cool, humid conditions.
  • It is historically associated with:
  • Coal smoke.
  • Sulphur dioxide.
  • Fog.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Classical Smog → Coal + SO₂ + Fog

27. Photochemical Smog
  • Photochemical smog forms mainly in sunny urban environments.
  • It develops through reactions involving:
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • VOCs.
  • Sunlight.
28. Photochemical Smog Products

Important components include:

  • Ground-level ozone.
  • Peroxyacyl nitrates.
  • Secondary aerosols.
29. Temperature Inversion
  • Normally, air temperature decreases with height in the lower atmosphere.
  • During an inversion, warmer air lies above cooler surface air.
  • This can trap pollution near the ground.
📌 Must-Memorise

Temperature Inversion → Traps Air Pollution

30. Indoor Air Pollution

Sources include:

  • Biomass cooking fuels.
  • Tobacco smoke.
  • Poor ventilation.
  • Chemicals.
  • Dust.
31. Vehicular Pollution

Vehicles emit pollutants such as:

  • Carbon monoxide.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • Particulate matter.
  • Hydrocarbons.
32. Industrial Air Pollution

Industries may release:

  • SO₂.
  • NOx.
  • Particulates.
  • VOCs.
  • Heavy metals.
33. Thermal Power and Air Pollution

Coal-fired power stations can release:

  • Carbon dioxide.
  • Sulphur dioxide.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • Fly ash.
  • Fine particulate matter.
34. Air Pollution Control

Important measures include:

  • Cleaner fuels.
  • Public transport.
  • Emission controls.
  • Industrial filters.
  • Renewable energy.
  • Energy efficiency.
  • Dust control.
35. Electrostatic Precipitator
  • An electrostatic precipitator removes fine particles from industrial exhaust gases using electrical charges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ESP → Removes Particulate Matter

36. Scrubber
  • Scrubbers remove certain gases and particles from industrial exhaust.
  • Wet scrubbers use liquid to capture pollutants.
37. Catalytic Converter
  • A catalytic converter reduces harmful vehicle exhaust pollutants.
  • It helps convert:
  • Carbon monoxide.
  • Hydrocarbons.
  • Nitrogen oxides.

into less harmful products.

38. Air Quality Index
  • AQI converts concentrations of major air pollutants into a simplified air-quality indicator.
  • Higher AQI generally indicates poorer air quality.
39. Water Pollution
  • Water pollution occurs when contaminants degrade the physical, chemical or biological quality of water.
  • It can make water unsafe for:
  • Drinking.
  • Agriculture.
  • Aquatic life.
40. Major Sources of Water Pollution

Sources include:

  • Domestic sewage.
  • Industrial effluents.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Mining.
  • Oil spills.
  • Solid waste.
41. Sewage Pollution

Untreated sewage contains:

  • Organic matter.
  • Disease-causing organisms.
  • Nutrients.
  • Suspended solids.
42. Biochemical Oxygen Demand
  • BOD measures the amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to decompose biodegradable organic matter.
  • High BOD generally indicates high organic pollution.
📌 Must-Memorise

High BOD → High Organic Pollution

43. Dissolved Oxygen
  • Dissolved oxygen is oxygen present in water.
  • Aquatic animals depend on adequate dissolved oxygen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Healthy Water → Higher DO

Organic Pollution → BOD ↑, DO ↓

44. Chemical Oxygen Demand
  • COD measures oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water.
  • It is another indicator of pollution load.
45. Eutrophication
  • Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of a water body.
  • Excess nitrogen and phosphorus stimulate excessive algal and plant growth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eutrophication → Excess Nutrients

46. Algal Bloom
  • An algal bloom is rapid growth of algae in water.
  • Decomposition of large blooms can reduce dissolved oxygen.
47. Sources of Eutrophication

Major sources include:

  • Fertiliser runoff.
  • Sewage.
  • Detergents containing nutrients.
48. Agricultural Runoff

Runoff may carry:

  • Fertilisers.
  • Pesticides.
  • Sediments.

into rivers and lakes.

49. Industrial Water Pollution

Industrial wastewater may contain:

  • Acids.
  • Alkalis.
  • Heavy metals.
  • Organic chemicals.
  • Dyes.
  • Toxic substances.
50. Heavy Metal Pollution

Important toxic heavy metals include:

  • Mercury.
  • Lead.
  • Cadmium.
  • Chromium.
51. Mercury Pollution
  • Mercury can accumulate in aquatic organisms.
  • Certain forms such as methylmercury can biomagnify through food chains.
52. Biomagnification
  • Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of persistent pollutants at higher trophic levels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Biomagnification → Concentration ↑ Up Food Chain

53. Bioaccumulation
  • Bioaccumulation is the buildup of a pollutant within an individual organism over time.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bioaccumulation → One Organism

Biomagnification → Food Chain

54. Oil Pollution

Oil spills affect:

  • Seabirds.
  • Fish.
  • Mangroves.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Coastal livelihoods.
55. Groundwater Pollution

Groundwater may become polluted by:

  • Sewage leakage.
  • Industrial waste.
  • Agricultural chemicals.
  • Landfills.
56. Nitrate Pollution
  • Excess nitrate in groundwater commonly results from:
  • Fertilisers.
  • Sewage.
  • Animal waste.
57. Fluoride — Water-Quality Issue
  • Excess fluoride in groundwater can cause fluorosis.
  • Fluoride problems occur naturally in groundwater in parts of India.
58. Arsenic — Water-Quality Issue
  • Arsenic contamination is a serious groundwater problem in parts of the Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial region.
59. Water-Pollution Control

Important measures include:

  • Sewage treatment.
  • Effluent treatment.
  • Reduced chemical runoff.
  • Industrial regulation.
  • Wetland conservation.
  • Solid-waste control.
60. Sewage Treatment

Typical stages include:

  • Primary treatment.
  • Secondary treatment.
  • Advanced or tertiary treatment where required.
61. Primary Treatment
  • Primary treatment mainly removes:
  • Large solids.
  • Floating material.
  • Suspended solids.

through physical processes.

62. Secondary Treatment
  • Secondary treatment uses microorganisms to decompose biodegradable organic matter.
63. Tertiary Treatment
  • Tertiary treatment provides additional removal of:
  • Nutrients.
  • Pathogens.
  • Specific pollutants.
64. Effluent Treatment Plant
  • ETP treats industrial wastewater before discharge or reuse.
📌 Must-Memorise

ETP → Industrial Effluent Treatment

65. Common Effluent Treatment Plant
  • CETPs serve groups of industries, especially industrial clusters where individual treatment may be difficult.
66. Soil Pollution

Soil pollution occurs when harmful substances accumulate in soil.

Sources include:

  • Pesticides.
  • Industrial waste.
  • Heavy metals.
  • Plastics.
  • Sewage sludge.
  • Mining waste.
67. Effects of Soil Pollution

Soil pollution can:

  • Reduce fertility.
  • Contaminate crops.
  • Pollute groundwater.
  • Harm soil organisms.
68. Pesticide Pollution

Excess pesticide use can:

  • Harm non-target organisms.
  • Contaminate soil and water.
  • Accumulate in food chains.
69. Fertiliser Pollution

Excess fertiliser may lead to:

  • Nitrate contamination.
  • Eutrophication.
  • Soil nutrient imbalance.
70. Solid Waste

Solid waste includes:

  • Household waste.
  • Commercial waste.
  • Industrial waste.
  • Construction debris.
  • Electronic waste.
71. Municipal Solid Waste

Municipal waste commonly contains:

  • Food waste.
  • Paper.
  • Plastics.
  • Glass.
  • Metals.
  • Textiles.
72. Waste Segregation

Waste should ideally be separated at source into appropriate categories such as:

  • Biodegradable.
  • Recyclable.
  • Hazardous.
73. Biodegradable Waste

Examples include:

  • Food waste.
  • Garden waste.
  • Agricultural organic matter.
74. Non-Biodegradable Waste

Examples include:

  • Many plastics.
  • Glass.
  • Metals.
75. Composting
  • Composting is controlled biological decomposition of organic waste.
  • The product can be used as soil amendment.
76. Vermicomposting
  • Vermicomposting uses earthworms to convert organic waste into nutrient-rich compost.
77. Anaerobic Digestion
  • Anaerobic digestion breaks down organic waste without oxygen.
  • It produces:
  • Biogas.
  • Digestate.
78. Landfill
  • A sanitary landfill is an engineered site for controlled disposal of waste.
  • Poorly managed dumps can contaminate:
  • Soil.
  • Groundwater.
  • Air.
79. Leachate
  • Leachate is contaminated liquid formed when water passes through waste.
📌 Must-Memorise

Leachate → Polluted Liquid from Waste

80. Landfill Gas

Landfills can generate:

  • Methane.
  • Carbon dioxide.

from decomposition of organic material.

81. Incineration
  • Incineration burns waste at high temperatures.
  • It reduces waste volume but requires emission control.
82. Waste-to-Energy
  • Waste-to-energy systems recover useful energy from suitable waste.
  • Proper segregation and pollution control are essential.
83. E-Waste

Electronic waste includes discarded:

  • Computers.
  • Phones.
  • Televisions.
  • Electronic appliances.
84. E-Waste Hazards

E-waste may contain:

  • Lead.
  • Mercury.
  • Cadmium.
  • Flame retardants.
  • Valuable recoverable metals.
85. Biomedical Waste

Biomedical waste originates from:

  • Hospitals.
  • Clinics.
  • Laboratories.
  • Veterinary facilities.

It may contain infectious or hazardous material.

86. Hazardous Waste

Hazardous waste can be:

  • Toxic.
  • Corrosive.
  • Reactive.
  • Flammable.
87. Plastic Pollution

Plastic pollution affects:

  • Soil.
  • Rivers.
  • Oceans.
  • Wildlife.
88. Microplastics
  • Microplastics are very small plastic particles.
  • They occur in:
  • Rivers.
  • Oceans.
  • Soil.
  • Food chains.
89. Marine Pollution

Major marine pollutants include:

  • Plastics.
  • Sewage.
  • Oil.
  • Industrial chemicals.
  • Agricultural runoff.
90. Dead Zone
  • A dead zone is an area of very low dissolved oxygen in water.
  • Nutrient pollution and eutrophication can contribute to its formation.
91. Noise Pollution
  • Noise pollution is unwanted or harmful sound.
  • Major sources include:
  • Traffic.
  • Aircraft.
  • Industries.
  • Construction.
  • Loudspeakers.
92. Decibel
  • Sound intensity level is commonly measured in decibels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Noise → Decibel

93. Effects of Noise Pollution

Excessive noise can cause:

  • Hearing loss.
  • Stress.
  • Sleep disturbance.
  • Reduced concentration.
94. Noise-Pollution Control

Measures include:

  • Silence zones.
  • Vehicle maintenance.
  • Sound barriers.
  • Land-use planning.
  • Restrictions on excessive loudspeaker use.
95. Thermal Pollution
  • Thermal pollution occurs when human activities significantly change the temperature of natural water bodies.
  • Power stations and industries may discharge heated water.
96. Effect of Thermal Pollution

Warmer water generally:

  • Holds less dissolved oxygen.
  • Alters aquatic ecosystems.
  • Can stress fish.
97. Radioactive Pollution

Sources include:

  • Nuclear accidents.
  • Radioactive waste.
  • Mining of radioactive minerals.
  • Improper handling of radioactive materials.
98. Radiation Effects

High exposure can damage:

  • Cells.
  • DNA.
  • Tissues.

Long-lived radioactive materials require careful containment.

99. Acid Rain
  • Acid rain forms when sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react in the atmosphere to produce acidic compounds.
📌 Must-Memorise

Acid Rain → SO₂ + NOx

100. Effects of Acid Rain

Acid rain can damage:

  • Lakes.
  • Forests.
  • Crops.
  • Buildings.
  • Monuments.
101. Taj Mahal and Air Pollution
  • Air pollution around the Agra region has long been a concern because pollutants can contribute to deterioration and discolouration of marble structures.
102. Ozone Layer
  • The ozone layer lies mainly in the stratosphere.
  • It absorbs much of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
📌 Must-Memorise

Stratospheric Ozone → UV Protection

103. Ozone Depletion
  • Ozone depletion refers to reduction in stratospheric ozone concentration.
  • Chlorofluorocarbons were major ozone-depleting substances.
104. CFCs
  • CFC means chlorofluorocarbon.
  • CFCs were historically used in:
  • Refrigeration.
  • Aerosols.
  • Foam production.
105. Ozone Hole
  • Severe seasonal ozone depletion is especially associated with Antarctica.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ozone Hole → Antarctica

106. Montreal Protocol
  • The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987.
  • It aims to phase out ozone-depleting substances.
📌 Must-Memorise

Montreal Protocol → 1987 → Ozone Layer

107. Kigali Amendment
  • The Kigali Amendment was adopted in 2016.
  • It addresses phased reduction of hydrofluorocarbons.
  • HFCs generally do not deplete ozone significantly but many are powerful greenhouse gases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kigali Amendment → HFCs

108. Greenhouse Effect
  • The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth's lower atmosphere caused by gases that absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation.
  • The natural greenhouse effect is essential for maintaining habitable temperatures.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Greenhouse Effect → Natural Process

Enhanced Greenhouse Effect → Human-Driven Additional Warming

109. Greenhouse Gases

Important greenhouse gases include:

  • Carbon dioxide.
  • Methane.
  • Nitrous oxide.
  • Water vapour.
  • Ozone.
  • Fluorinated gases.
110. Carbon Dioxide

Major human sources include:

  • Fossil-fuel combustion.
  • Cement production.
  • Deforestation.
111. Methane

Important methane sources include:

  • Wetlands.
  • Livestock.
  • Rice fields.
  • Landfills.
  • Fossil-fuel production.
112. Nitrous Oxide

Important human sources include:

  • Nitrogen fertilisers.
  • Agricultural soils.
  • Industrial processes.
113. Water Vapour
  • Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas.
  • Its atmospheric concentration strongly responds to temperature, making it an important climate feedback.
114. Global Warming
  • Global warming refers to the long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, especially due to increased greenhouse-gas concentrations from human activities.
115. Climate Change
  • Climate change refers to persistent long-term changes in climate patterns.
  • It includes changes in:
  • Temperature.
  • Rainfall.
  • Extreme weather.
  • Sea level.
  • Cryosphere.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Global Warming → Temperature Increase

Climate Change → Wider Set of Climate Changes

116. Weather vs Climate

Weather:

  • Short-term atmospheric condition.

Climate:

  • Long-term statistical pattern of weather.
117. Anthropogenic Climate Change

Major human causes include:

  • Fossil-fuel use.
  • Deforestation.
  • Industrial activity.
  • Agriculture.
  • Land-use change.
118. Carbon Cycle

Major carbon reservoirs include:

  • Atmosphere.
  • Oceans.
  • Vegetation.
  • Soil.
  • Rocks.
119. Carbon Sink
  • A carbon sink absorbs more carbon than it releases.
  • Major sinks include:
  • Oceans.
  • Forests.
  • Soils.
120. Carbon Source
  • A carbon source releases more carbon than it absorbs.
121. Carbon Sequestration
  • Carbon sequestration means capturing and storing carbon.
  • It may occur:
  • Naturally in forests and soils.
  • Technologically through carbon-capture systems.
122. Carbon Footprint
  • Carbon footprint represents greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an activity, person, product or organisation.
123. Carbon Neutrality
  • Carbon neutrality means balancing carbon dioxide emissions with equivalent removals or offsets under a defined accounting framework.
124. Net Zero
  • Net zero generally means reducing greenhouse-gas emissions as far as possible and balancing remaining emissions with removals.
  • It is broader than simply reducing energy consumption.
125. Climate Feedback
  • A feedback is a process that amplifies or reduces an initial climate change.
126. Ice-Albedo Feedback
  • Ice and snow reflect sunlight.
  • Melting reduces surface reflectivity.
  • Darker surfaces absorb more heat.
  • This can amplify warming.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ice Melt → Albedo ↓ → Heat Absorption ↑

127. Albedo
  • Albedo is the fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface.
  • Snow and ice have high albedo.
128. Sea-Level Rise

Sea level rises mainly because of:

  • Thermal expansion of warming seawater.
  • Melting of land ice.
129. Thermal Expansion
  • Water expands as it warms.
  • Ocean warming therefore contributes to sea-level rise.
130. Glacier Retreat
  • Rising temperatures are affecting many mountain glaciers.
  • Himalayan glacier changes can influence seasonal water availability.
131. Climate Change and Indian Monsoon

Climate change can influence:

  • Rainfall intensity.
  • Spatial distribution.
  • Extreme rainfall events.
  • Dry spells.

The monsoon response is complex and varies by region.

132. Climate Change and Heat Waves
  • Rising average temperatures increase the likelihood and severity of extreme heat in many regions.
133. Climate Change and Drought

Climate change can influence drought through:

  • Rainfall changes.
  • Higher evaporation.
  • Soil-moisture loss.
134. Climate Change and Floods

Warmer air can hold more moisture, contributing under suitable conditions to:

  • More intense rainfall.
  • Greater flash-flood and urban-flood risk.
135. Climate Change and Cyclones
  • Tropical cyclone impacts can be influenced by ocean warming and sea-level rise.
  • Warmer seas can support intense cyclonic systems when other atmospheric conditions are favourable.
136. Climate Change and Agriculture

Potential impacts include:

  • Heat stress.
  • Changed growing seasons.
  • Altered rainfall.
  • Greater irrigation demand.
  • Pest changes.
  • Yield variability.
137. Climate Change and Wheat
  • Excess heat during grain formation can reduce wheat yield.
  • Northwestern Indian wheat is vulnerable to unusually high late-season temperatures.
138. Climate Change and Rice

Rice cultivation can be affected by:

  • Heat.
  • Water stress.
  • Flooding.
  • Salinity in coastal areas.
139. Climate Change and Fisheries

Potential impacts include:

  • Ocean warming.
  • Changes in fish distribution.
  • Coral bleaching.
  • Ocean acidification.
140. Ocean Acidification
  • Oceans absorb carbon dioxide.
  • Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ocean Acidification → CO₂ Absorption → pH Falls

141. Ocean Acidification and Corals
  • Lower pH reduces availability of carbonate ions needed by many shell-forming and reef-building organisms.
142. Coral Bleaching
  • Heat stress can cause corals to lose symbiotic algae.
  • Severe or prolonged bleaching can lead to coral mortality.
143. Climate Change and Biodiversity

Species may respond by:

  • Moving poleward.
  • Moving uphill.
  • Changing breeding periods.
  • Changing migration patterns.
144. Mountain Species
  • Species restricted to high elevations may face habitat loss if climatic zones shift upward.
145. Climate Change and Mangroves

Mangroves face:

  • Sea-level rise.
  • Coastal development.
  • Salinity changes.
  • Extreme storms.

Where space exists, mangroves may migrate inland.

146. Climate Change and Human Health

Potential effects include:

  • Heat stress.
  • Expanded disease-vector ranges.
  • Malnutrition.
  • Air-quality problems.
147. Climate Mitigation
  • Mitigation means reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing greenhouse-gas removal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mitigation → Causes of Climate Change

148. Climate Adaptation
  • Adaptation means adjusting human or natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Adaptation → Effects of Climate Change

149. Mitigation vs Adaptation

Mitigation:

  • Renewable energy.
  • Energy efficiency.
  • Afforestation.

Adaptation:

  • Drought-resistant crops.
  • Flood protection.
  • Heat-action plans.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mitigation → Reduce Warming

Adaptation → Live with Impacts

150. Climate Resilience
  • Climate resilience is the capacity to anticipate, withstand and recover from climate-related stresses.
151. Afforestation
  • Afforestation establishes tree cover on land that was not recently forested.
  • Trees can store atmospheric carbon.
152. Reforestation
  • Reforestation restores forests on previously forested land.
153. Blue Carbon
  • Blue carbon is carbon stored in coastal ecosystems such as:
  • Mangroves.
  • Seagrasses.
  • Salt marshes.
154. Climate-Smart Agriculture

Measures include:

  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Drought-tolerant varieties.
  • Crop diversification.
  • Soil-carbon improvement.
  • Weather advisories.
155. Urban Climate Adaptation

Important measures include:

  • Urban trees.
  • Cool roofs.
  • Wetland protection.
  • Storm-water drainage.
  • Heat-action plans.
156. Cool Roof
  • A cool roof reflects more sunlight and absorbs less heat than a conventional dark roof.
  • It can reduce indoor and urban heat stress.
157. Green Building

Green buildings aim to reduce:

  • Energy use.
  • Water use.
  • Waste.
  • Environmental impact.
158. International Climate Framework

Major international milestones include:

  • UNFCCC → 1992.
  • Kyoto Protocol → 1997.
  • Paris Agreement → 2015.
📌 Must-Memorise

UNFCCC → 1992

Kyoto → 1997

Paris → 2015

159. UNFCCC
  • UNFCCC stands for United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.
  • It provides the main international framework for cooperation on climate change.
160. Kyoto Protocol
  • Kyoto Protocol established binding emission-reduction commitments for specified developed countries under the UNFCCC framework.
161. Paris Agreement
  • The Paris Agreement seeks to strengthen the global response to climate change.
  • It aims to keep warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C.
📌 Must-Memorise

  • NDCs are national climate-action commitments submitted under the Paris Agreement.

  • COP means Conference of the Parties.

  • Impacts.

  • Mitigation.

  • Geothermal.

  • Renewable energy comes from naturally replenished sources.

  • Solar electricity replaces part of fossil-fuel-based generation without direct fuel combustion.

  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.

  • Solar thermal technologies use solar heat.

  • Wind turbines convert kinetic energy of air into electricity.

  • Hydroelectricity is renewable because it depends on the water cycle.

  • River fragmentation.

  • Small hydropower generally uses smaller flows and structures.

Biomass sources include:

  • Biomass is renewable only when its biological source is replenished sustainably.

Energy-efficient buildings use:

Public transport can reduce:

  • Coastal hazards.

Potential risks include:

  • Sea-level rise.

  • Agricultural water stress.

Potential impacts include:

High-elevation ecosystems may be vulnerable to:

Important examples include:

  • Kamuthi in Ramanathapuram district is associated with large-scale solar-power development.

217. Solar Potential in Tamil Nadu

Favourable areas include dry regions with:

  • Palghat Gap channels winds toward western Tamil Nadu.

220. Aralvaimozhi Pass

Replacing fossil-fuel combustion with low-emission energy can reduce:

Challenges include:

  • EIA evaluates likely environmental impacts of a proposed project before approval and implementation.

227. Environmental Monitoring

Monitoring tracks changes in:

  • Water quality.
  • Soil.
  • Noise.

228. Polluter Pays Principle
  • The polluter-pays principle states that those responsible for pollution should bear the cost of preventing and remedying environmental damage.
229. Precautionary Principle
  • The precautionary principle supports preventive action where serious environmental harm is possible even when scientific certainty is incomplete.
230. Sustainable Development
  • Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
231. Environmental Sustainability

Environmental sustainability requires:

  • Resource conservation.
  • Pollution control.
  • Biodiversity protection.
  • Efficient energy use.
  • Climate resilience.
232. TNPSC High-Yield Pollution Pairings
  • PM2.5 → Fine particles.
  • CO → Incomplete combustion.
  • SO₂ → Acid rain.
  • NOx → Smog + acid rain.
  • Ground ozone → Secondary pollutant.
  • ESP → Particulate removal.
  • BOD → Organic pollution.
  • Eutrophication → Nutrient enrichment.
  • Leachate → Landfill liquid.
  • Decibel → Noise.
  • CFC → Ozone depletion.
  • Montreal Protocol → Ozone.
  • Kigali Amendment → HFCs.
  • Biomagnification → Food chain.
233. TNPSC High-Yield Climate Pairings
  • CO₂ → Fossil fuels.
  • CH₄ → Livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills.
  • N₂O → Fertilisers.
  • Albedo → Reflectivity.
  • Sea-level rise → Thermal expansion + land-ice melt.
  • Mitigation → Reduce causes.
  • Adaptation → Manage impacts.
  • UNFCCC → 1992.
  • Kyoto → 1997.
  • Paris → 2015.
  • IPCC → Climate assessment.
234. Tamil Nadu High-Yield Pairings
  • Cooum → Chennai pollution.
  • Adyar → Chennai urban river.
  • Noyyal → Tiruppur industrial belt.
  • Tannery → Chromium pollution.
  • Gulf of Mannar → Coral + seagrass.
  • Muppandal → Wind.
  • Kamuthi → Solar.
  • Kadamparai → Pumped storage.
  • Palghat Gap → Wind corridor.
  • Kaveri Delta → Climate/coastal vulnerability.
235. TNPSC Traps
  • Pollutant may be matter or energy.
  • Primary and secondary pollutants are different.
  • PM2.5 is finer than PM10.
  • Carbon monoxide is not carbon dioxide.
  • CO forms mainly through incomplete combustion.
  • Ground-level ozone is harmful, while stratospheric ozone protects against UV.
  • Temperature inversion can trap pollutants.
  • High BOD usually indicates high organic pollution.
  • High BOD generally reduces dissolved oxygen.
  • Eutrophication results from nutrient enrichment.
  • Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are different.
  • Leachate is liquid from waste, not landfill gas.
  • Noise is measured in decibels.
  • Acid rain is associated mainly with SO₂ and NOx.
  • CFCs cause ozone depletion.
  • Montreal Protocol deals with ozone depletion, not climate change in general.
  • Kigali Amendment targets HFC reduction.
  • Global warming and climate change are not identical.
  • Natural greenhouse effect is necessary for life.
  • Enhanced greenhouse effect causes additional warming.
  • Sea-level rise results from both thermal expansion and land-ice melt.
  • Mitigation and adaptation are different.
  • Renewable energy is not impact-free.
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier.
  • Pumped hydro is energy storage.
  • Green hydrogen uses renewable-powered electrolysis.
  • EVs have zero tailpipe emissions but not automatically zero life-cycle emissions.
236. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • PM2.5 → Fine.
  • CO → Incomplete combustion.
  • SO₂ → Acid rain.
  • NOx → Smog.
  • O₃ ground → Pollutant.
  • O₃ stratosphere → Protection.
  • Inversion → Pollution trapped.
  • BOD high → Pollution high.
  • DO low → Bad water.
  • Nutrients → Eutrophication.
  • Leachate → Landfill liquid.
  • Noise → Decibel.
  • CFC → Ozone depletion.
  • Montreal → 1987.
  • Kigali → 2016.
  • CO₂ → Warming.
  • CH₄ → Methane.
  • Albedo → Reflection.
  • Mitigation → Causes.
  • Adaptation → Effects.
  • UNFCCC → 1992.
  • Kyoto → 1997.
  • Paris → 2015.
  • Solar → Kamuthi.
  • Wind → Muppandal.
  • Pumped storage → Kadamparai.
  • Noyyal → Tiruppur.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is environmental pollution? → Harmful alteration of environmental quality.
  • What is a pollutant? → Substance or energy causing harmful environmental effects.
  • What is a primary pollutant? → Pollutant emitted directly.
  • What is a secondary pollutant? → Pollutant formed through environmental chemical reactions.
  • Example of secondary air pollutant? → Ground-level ozone.
  • What is point-source pollution? → Pollution from a clearly identifiable source.
  • What is non-point-source pollution? → Diffuse pollution from widespread sources.
  • PM10 means? → Particles up to about 10 micrometres.
  • PM2.5 means? → Fine particles up to about 2.5 micrometres.
  • Which is finer, PM2.5 or PM10? → PM2.5.
  • Carbon monoxide is produced mainly by? → Incomplete combustion.
  • Why is CO dangerous? → It reduces oxygen transport by binding haemoglobin.
  • Main sources of SO₂? → Sulphur-containing fossil-fuel combustion.
  • SO₂ contributes to? → Acid rain and particulate pollution.
  • NOx contributes to? → Smog, ozone and acid rain.
  • What is photochemical smog? → Sunlight-driven pollution involving NOx and VOCs.
  • What is classical smog associated with? → Coal smoke, SO₂ and fog.
  • What is temperature inversion? → Warm air over cool surface air that can trap pollution.
  • What does an electrostatic precipitator remove? → Particulate matter.
  • What is a catalytic converter used for? → Reducing vehicle-exhaust pollutants.
  • What does AQI indicate? → Overall air-quality condition.
  • What is BOD? → Oxygen required by microbes to decompose biodegradable organic matter.
  • What does high BOD indicate? → High organic pollution.
  • Relation between BOD and dissolved oxygen? → High BOD generally causes lower DO.
  • What is eutrophication? → Excess nutrient enrichment of water.
  • Main nutrients responsible for eutrophication? → Nitrogen and phosphorus compounds.
  • What is biomagnification? → Increasing pollutant concentration at higher trophic levels.
  • What is bioaccumulation? → Pollutant accumulation within an organism.
  • What is leachate? → Polluted liquid draining through waste.
  • What is composting? → Biological conversion of organic waste into compost.
  • What is vermicomposting? → Composting using earthworms.
  • What is e-waste? → Discarded electrical and electronic equipment.
  • What are microplastics? → Very small plastic particles.
  • Noise is measured in? → Decibels.
  • What is thermal pollution? → Harmful temperature alteration of a water body.
  • Acid rain is mainly caused by? → Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
  • Where is the ozone layer concentrated? → Stratosphere.
  • Main function of stratospheric ozone? → Absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
  • CFCs are associated with? → Ozone depletion.
  • Ozone hole is especially associated with? → Antarctica.
  • Montreal Protocol adopted in? → 1987.
  • Montreal Protocol deals with? → Ozone-depleting substances.
  • Kigali Amendment adopted in? → 2016.
  • Kigali Amendment deals mainly with? → HFC phase-down.
  • What is greenhouse effect? → Atmospheric trapping and re-emission of outgoing infrared radiation.
  • Is the natural greenhouse effect harmful? → No; it keeps Earth warm enough for life.
  • Main anthropogenic greenhouse gas from fossil-fuel burning? → Carbon dioxide.
  • Main component of biogas and an important greenhouse gas? → Methane.
  • Which greenhouse gas is strongly linked with fertiliser use? → Nitrous oxide.
  • What is global warming? → Long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature.
  • Difference between global warming and climate change? → Global warming refers mainly to temperature rise; climate change includes broader long-term climatic changes.
  • What is a carbon sink? → System absorbing more carbon than it releases.
  • Major carbon sinks? → Oceans, forests and soils.
  • What is carbon sequestration? → Capture and long-term storage of carbon.
  • What is carbon footprint? → Greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an activity or product.
  • What is albedo? → Surface reflectivity.
  • Why does melting ice amplify warming? → Lower albedo causes more solar-energy absorption.
  • Two major causes of sea-level rise? → Thermal expansion and melting of land ice.
  • What is ocean acidification? → Decline in ocean pH due largely to absorption of atmospheric CO₂.
  • What is climate mitigation? → Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing removals.
  • What is climate adaptation? → Adjusting to climate impacts.
  • Give one mitigation example. → Renewable energy.
  • Give one adaptation example. → Drought-resistant crops.
  • UNFCCC adopted in? → 1992.
  • Kyoto Protocol adopted in? → 1997.
  • Paris Agreement adopted in? → 2015.
  • Paris temperature objective? → Well below 2°C while pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C.
  • IPCC full form? → Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
  • What does IPCC do? → Assesses climate-change science, impacts, adaptation and mitigation.
  • What is renewable energy? → Energy from naturally replenished sources.
  • Main green-energy sources? → Solar, wind, hydro, sustainable biomass and geothermal.
  • What does photovoltaic mean? → Direct conversion of sunlight into electricity.
  • What is green hydrogen? → Hydrogen produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity.
  • Is hydrogen a primary energy resource? → No, it is an energy carrier.
  • What is pumped-storage hydropower? → Electricity storage by pumping water uphill and releasing it later.
  • Tamil Nadu pumped-storage location? → Kadamparai.
  • Tamil Nadu famous wind centre? → Muppandal.
  • Muppandal is in which district? → Kanyakumari.
  • Tamil Nadu solar location strongly associated with Ramanathapuram? → Kamuthi.
  • Which gap helps create wind corridors in western Tamil Nadu? → Palghat Gap.
  • International Solar Alliance was initiated by? → India and France.
  • Year associated with International Solar Alliance launch? → 2015.
  • What are the 3Rs? → Reduce, Reuse and Recycle.
  • What is EIA? → Environmental Impact Assessment.
  • What is the polluter-pays principle? → Polluter bears the cost of pollution control and damage.
  • What is the precautionary principle? → Preventive action may be taken where serious environmental harm is possible despite uncertainty.
  • Major polluted urban waterways of Chennai? → Cooum, Adyar and Buckingham Canal.
  • Which Tamil Nadu river is strongly associated with Tiruppur's industrial pollution issue? → Noyyal.
  • Which pollutant is a major concern in tannery wastewater? → Chromium.
  • Why is Gulf of Mannar environmentally important? → Coral reefs, seagrasses, dugongs and marine biodiversity.
  • Major climate risks for the Kaveri delta? → Sea-level rise, salinity, cyclones and rainfall variability.
  • Why are solar and wind useful for air-pollution control? → They generate electricity without direct fossil-fuel combustion.
